cards.power: Gatekeeper's Toll – Exhausts 3 opponent attention tokens by forcing them to wait 10 years for a completely arbitrary paradigm shift.
cards.lore: Since 1952, the Sight & Sound cabal of critics summons itself every decade to dictate global taste. 1,639 critics participated in 2022 to remind you that your favorite movie is trash.

cards.power: Auteur's Hubris – Steals all credit from the writer and crew tokens. Automatically counters any criticism by claiming it's about the process.
cards.lore: Added in 1992, the directors' separate poll proves that filmmakers completely disagree with critics. 480 directors voted in 2022 to elevate their own cinematic kayfabe above the journalists.

cards.power: Nostalgia Farm – Extracts infinite financial capital by repeating the same comfortable formula. Destroys all nuance tokens in play.
cards.lore: Audience polls repeatedly vote for Star Wars or The Godfather. The masses demand the myth they have already purchased.

cards.power: Echo Chamber – Grants invulnerability to any film produced within the player's own borders. Ignores all international context.
cards.lore: National polls exist primarily to validate local funding. Every nation has a mathematically proven greatest film that no one outside its borders has ever seen.

cards.power: Rosebud Extraction – Forces all opponents to spend their turn debating the symbolic meaning of a child's toy. Generates 5 Pretension Points.
cards.lore: Topped the Sight & Sound poll for five consecutive decades (1962–2002). 46 critics in 2002 maintained the ultimate kayfabe: that a movie about a newspaper tycoon is the peak of human art.

cards.power: Obsessive Sabotage – Target player becomes dizzy, replaying the exact same trauma loop for 3 turns while dressing up a companion token.
cards.lore: Dethroned the Kane dog in 2012 when 191 critics decided Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo—a film about male obsession and heights—was the new objective truth.

cards.power: Durational Labor – Forces all opponents to skip 3 hours of real-time gameplay to experience the crushing weight of domestic drudgery.
cards.lore: Jeanne Dielman conquered the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll, weaponizing three hours of real-time kitchen chores to obliterate capitalist entertainment metrics.

cards.power: Neorealist Guilt – Drains all Joy tokens from the board. Opponents must donate half their resources out of pure, unadulterated pity.
cards.lore: Topped the very first Sight & Sound poll in 1952 with a mere 25 votes. Italian Neorealism proved that true cinematic power comes from making the audience feel terrible about post-war poverty.

cards.power: Evolutionary Bore – Upgrades player's intelligence stat but completely alienates them from everyone else at the table.
cards.lore: 2001: A Space Odyssey topped the 2022 directors' poll. Filmmakers united to decree that a slow-moving, dialogue-free void is the pinnacle of the moving image.

cards.power: Generational Guilt – Inflicts passive-aggressive damage. Opponents must instantly call their parents and apologize for being busy.
cards.lore: Yasujirō Ozu's Tokyo Story topped the 2012 directors' poll with 48 votes. The ultimate kayfabe that cinematic perfection is achieved by placing a camera two feet off the floor and not moving it.

cards.power: Mercenary Labor – Sacrifices your own units to protect a village of ungrateful peasant tokens. Grants immortal legendary status.
cards.lore: Seven Samurai (1954) was voted the greatest foreign-language film in a 2018 BBC poll of 209 critics. The foundation myth of every modern action ensemble, extracted from Japanese history.

cards.power: Creative Block – You may refuse to take your turn. Instead, gain points by loudly explaining why your inability to play is actually a masterpiece.
cards.lore: Fellini's 8½ topped the 2015 Łódź poll of 279 Polish film professionals. Directors love nothing more than watching a film about how incredibly hard it is to be a director.

cards.power: Historical Amnesia – Adjusts the rules of the past to suit the player. Generates massive wealth tokens while ignoring problematic lore.
cards.lore: Gone with the Wind was voted the favorite film of Americans in 2008 and 2014 Harris Interactive polls. The ultimate enduring myth of the American public, immune to critical re-evaluation.

cards.power: Offer Refusal – Forces opponent to instantly forfeit their hand, or wake up with their favorite card destroyed.
cards.lore: The Godfather was voted #1 by Entertainment Weekly, Time Out, and 20,000 Empire readers. The undisputed heavyweight champion of masculine fantasy projection.

cards.power: Merchandising Empire – Extracts real-world currency from opponents every time they feel a shred of childhood nostalgia.
cards.lore: The Empire Strikes Back was voted the best film of all time by over 250,000 Empire magazine readers. The kayfabe that sequel IP ownership is the highest art form.

cards.power: Tear Extraction – Floods the board. Opponents lose 2 turns weeping uncontrollably over entirely avoidable tragedies.
cards.lore: Titanic was voted the greatest hit of all time by 6,000 Chinese movie fans in a 2008 China Daily poll. A global phenomenon built on the extraction of pure teenage emotional labor.

cards.power: Faith Sabotage – Forces opponents to question their religious beliefs. Deals psychological damage that bypasses all shields.
cards.lore: The Exorcist was voted the best horror film by 150 experts in a 2012 Time Out poll. Weaponized Catholic guilt proven to be the most effective mechanism for cinematic terror.

cards.power: Holiday Hijack – Permanently reclassifies any opponent's peaceful phase into an explosive combat zone. Yippee-ki-yay.
cards.lore: Voted the best action film by Time Out New York and the greatest Christmas movie by Empire readers. The myth that an everyman can defeat European terrorists with no shoes on.

cards.power: Perfect Imperfection – Nullifies any penalty by declaring Nobody's perfect! Gains immunity to critical logic.
cards.lore: Some Like It Hot was voted the best comedy in a poll of 253 global critics by the BBC in 2017. A masterpiece of cross-dressing survival kayfabe.

cards.power: Deceptive Whimsy – Tells a lie that looks beautiful. Opponents lose resources believing in wishing stars while turning into donkeys.
cards.lore: Pinocchio was voted the best animated movie by Time Out in 2014. The animation industry's foundational kayfabe: extracting soul from graphite and ink.

cards.power: Bourgeois Collapse – Causes all high-society tokens to destroy themselves in a misunderstanding over a romantic affair.
cards.lore: Voted the best French film by Time Out Paris and the best European film by Cinemateca Portuguesa. Jean Renoir's ultimate exposé of upper-class societal kayfabe.

cards.power: Copyright Infringement – Drains the blood from the original source material. Survives even if a court orders all your cards destroyed.
cards.lore: Tied for best European film in the 1994 Cinemateca Portuguesa poll. An illegal rip-off of Dracula that survived by sheer, unadulterated visual trauma.

cards.power: Montage Shock – Smashes two unrelated cards together to force a new, highly propagandistic emotional response from the opponent.
cards.lore: Battleship Potemkin topped the 1951 Brussels World's Fair poll. Eisenstein's kayfabe: inventing modern film editing just to legitimize a state revolution.

cards.power: Kino-Eye Truth – Strips all narrative illusions from the board. Forces opponents to look at raw, unscripted mechanical reality.
cards.lore: Man with a Movie Camera topped the 2014 Sight & Sound documentary poll. Dziga Vertov's radical assault on the very concept of fictional acting.

cards.power: Frontier Manifestation – Pushes opponent tokens out of their territory to establish your own heroic, highly sanitized national origin myth.
cards.lore: Voted best Western film in a 1996 Nickel Odeon poll of experts. John Ford's ultimate construction of the American geographic kayfabe.

cards.power: Tears in Rain – Your best cards are deleted upon expiration. Opponent must ponder what it means to be truly alive.
cards.lore: Blade Runner was voted the best sci-fi film by a panel of 56 scientists in The Guardian (2004). The scientists agreed: corporate dystopian depression is our most likely future.

cards.power: Unspoken Anguish – Prevents players from taking direct action. All combat must be resolved through repressed longing and societal pressure.
cards.lore: Brokeback Mountain topped the 2016 Time Out London poll for LGBT+ cinema. A masterclass in weaponizing the mythic masculine western against itself.

cards.power: Basic Cable Immortality – Even if defeated, this card returns to the board every single Sunday afternoon, completely unavoidable.
cards.lore: Voted the greatest film by Empire readers in 2006. The ultimate comfort kayfabe: the belief that patience and a rock hammer will conquer all systemic injustice.

cards.power: Humanist Revelation – Forces the opponent to stop playing the game and simply appreciate the tragic beauty of ordinary life.
cards.lore: Topped the British Film Institute's user poll of Top 10 Indian Films in 2002. Satyajit Ray's masterpiece that forced the West to admit cinema existed outside their bubble.

cards.power: Post-War Paralysis – Locks down the board. No player may attack; they can only sigh deeply and reflect on broken marriages.
cards.lore: Spring in a Small Town (1948) was ranked #1 by the Hong Kong Film Awards Association in 2005. A subtle, poetic sabotage of grand, noisy historical narratives.

cards.power: Domestic Subversion – Infiltrates the opponent's resource deck and slowly poisons it from the inside while cleaning their house.
cards.lore: The Housemaid (1960) topped a 2024 poll of 240 critics by the Korean Film Archive. The blueprint for Korean cinema's obsession with violent class warfare.

cards.power: Heroic Bloodshed – Generates infinite ammo tokens. Allows you to die in slow motion, guaranteeing you win the moral victory.
cards.lore: A Better Tomorrow (1986) was voted the second-best Chinese film ever. John Woo established the kayfabe that true brotherhood requires shooting 500 people in slow-mo.

cards.power: Bourgeois Alienation – Allows the player to observe the game losing without ever taking responsibility for the outcome.
cards.lore: Memories of Underdevelopment was voted best Latin American film by 36 critics in 1999. Tomás Gutiérrez Alea's documentation of the ultimate revolutionary spectator sport.

cards.power: Marginal Cinema – Flips the game rules upside down. Trash tokens become gold tokens; logic becomes an illegal move.
cards.lore: The Red Light Bandit (1968) was voted the best Brazilian film in a 2011 Filme Cultura poll. A frantic, anarchic middle finger to polished cinema aesthetics.

cards.power: Exploitation Backlash – When your health reaches zero, instantly destroy the opponent's most expensive, capital-generating unit.
cards.lore: Prisioneros de la tierra (1939) was repeatedly voted the greatest Argentine film by the Museo del Cine. A raw, blistering kayfabe exposing the extraction of indigenous labor.

cards.power: Disillusionment – Strips all Hero tags from opponent's cards. Everyone is revealed to be a flawed, violent opportunist.
cards.lore: Vámonos con Pancho Villa (1936) was ranked the #1 Mexican film in a 1994 Somos poll. It systematically dismantles the romantic kayfabe of revolutionary war.

cards.power: Unsolved Mystery – Leaves the game abruptly. The opponent spends the rest of the match trying to figure out what just happened.
cards.lore: Picnic at Hanging Rock was voted the best Australian film in a 1996 poll. The ultimate export of the Australian Gothic kayfabe: that the continent simply eats people.

cards.power: Generational Trauma – Deals heavy damage, but inflicts an equal amount of psychological recoil damage to your own deck.
cards.lore: Once Were Warriors was voted the best New Zealand film by a 2014 Fairfax Media poll. A brutal shattering of the picturesque, hobbit-filled New Zealand tourism myth.

cards.power: Cuckoo Clock Economics – Steals opponent's health potions and dilutes them, profiting off the post-war black market.
cards.lore: Voted the best British film ever in a 1999 BFI poll. Orson Welles stealing a movie with five minutes of screen time and a monologue about the Swiss.

cards.power: Flesh Wound – Refuses to be removed from the board even when completely destroyed. Continues to shout insults at the opponent.
cards.lore: Monty Python and the Holy Grail was voted the best British picture by 7,000 film fans (2004). The absolute pinnacle of unhinged, budget-less cinematic sabotage.

cards.power: Pagan Attrition – Confuses the opponent with three hours of non-linear, experimental narrative until they forfeit out of exhaustion.
cards.lore: Voted the best Czech film of all time by journalists in 1994 and 1998. The grand kayfabe that medieval brutality is best depicted through avant-garde poetry.

cards.power: Bureaucratic Sabotage – Opponent must fill out a form in triplicate before drawing a card. Failure results in immediate arrest.
cards.lore: Teddy Bear (1981) was voted the best movie by the public at 2013 Filmfest PL. Pure satirical venom aimed directly at the daily kayfabe of Communist absurdism.

cards.power: Psychological Enclosure – Reduces the board size every turn until the opponent has absolutely nowhere to move.
cards.lore: Voted the best Hungarian film in a 2000 critics' poll. Miklós Jancsó's masterclass in how to extract power through sheer, geometric intimidation.

cards.power: Deafening Roar – Mutes all sound in the game. Deals permanent psychic damage to whoever looks at the card too long.
cards.lore: Come and See was voted the best Belarusian film by 49 experts in 2024. The total, uncompromised destruction of the glorious war movie kayfabe.

cards.power: Tragic Rebellion – When destroyed, ignites a cultural revolution token that permanently changes the meta of the game.
cards.lore: The Deer (1974) was voted the best Iranian film in a 2009 poll of 92 critics. A fierce social critique that accidentally predicted and fueled an actual real-world revolution.

cards.power: Heritage Theft – Steals artifacts from the opponent's graveyard to sell for immediate, short-term survival points.
cards.lore: The Night of Counting the Years (1969) was voted the best Arab film by 475 professionals. The mythic clash between surviving the present and honoring the ancient dead.

cards.power: Draft Evasion – Ignores all combat phases. Gains points purely through comedic incompetence and avoiding authority.
cards.lore: Giv'at Halfon Eina Ona was voted Favorite Israeli Film by 25,000 web users. An absurdist deconstruction of the hyper-militarized national kayfabe.

cards.power: Resource Monopoly – Controls the water supply. Opponents must pay a heavy toll to un-tap any of their cards.
cards.lore: Dry Summer (1963) was voted the best Turkish film released between 1923-2013. A neo-realist exposé showing that controlling the water means controlling the myth.

cards.power: New Year's Penance – If played on the last turn, forces the opponent to review every mistake they made in the game and take guilt damage.
cards.lore: The Phantom Carriage (1921) was voted the best Swedish film by FLM magazine. Extracting morality from the audience by threatening them with the Grim Reaper's Uber service.

cards.power: Sisu Endurance – Refuses to die when HP hits zero. Survives purely out of stubborn, frozen spite.
cards.lore: The Unknown Soldier (1955) was voted the best Finnish movie by Helsingin Sanomat. The national kayfabe of surviving impossible odds through sheer, miserable grit.

cards.power: Pagan Return – Escapes the board's rules entirely to return to the earth deck. Cannot be targeted by modern corporate mechanics.
cards.lore: Children of Nature (1991) was voted the best Icelandic film. A rejection of modern, sterile aging in favor of merging with the mythological landscape.

cards.power: Criminal Incompetence – Attempting to attack usually results in the player accidentally blowing up their own resources, to the audience's delight.
cards.lore: Blinkende lygter was voted best Danish movie by the YouGov public poll. The kayfabe that violent gangsters are actually just lovable, quirky neurotics.

cards.power: Vote Stacking – Automatically wins any tie-breaker by utilizing skewed demographics and self-selection bias.
cards.lore: Wikipedia warns: Voting systems differ… surveys suffer from biases such as self-selection or skewed demographics, while others may be susceptible to interference. SEE?? BIAS!!

cards.power: Revisionist History – Changes the stats of a card played 10 turns ago because the current cultural meta demands it.
cards.lore: What was brilliant in 1952 is boring in 2022. The list is not a record of objective cinematic quality; it is a mirror reflecting the current anxieties of the electorate. THEY'RE ERASING THE PAST!!

cards.power: Categorical Dismissal – Prevents any Genre card from ever winning the Overall Best title, trapping them forever in their own specialized echo chamber.
cards.lore: Science fiction, horror, and comedy get their own lists because the serious decennial critics refuse to let aliens, ghosts, or laughter sit at the adult table. THE ELITES.

cards.power: Citation Needed – Nullifies any argument at the table by linking to an aggregate list of subjective opinions disguised as objective data.
cards.lore: List of films voted the best Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia. The ultimate motion picture kayfabe—compiling 100 years of global subjective art into a definitive, bloodless spreadsheet.
